q-kendwa-sand.name: Kendwa sand
q-kendwa-sand.teaser: Hotels straight onto three kilometres of public sand, and a man with green coconuts never far away
q-kendwa-sand.story: On Kendwa there is no road between your room and the sea: the hotels sit directly on the sand, and every one of them shares the same public beach. It runs from the Kendwa Rocks cluster north to the Kilindi headland, and you can walk it end to end in about twenty minutes. Public means company: vendors work it all day, which sounds like a nuisance until you discover the madafu trade, a green coconut opened in front of you, and the most useful thing anyone sells here. Why the water stays deep enough to swim is a story of its own, told under the tide.
q-kendwa-sand.why: Choose a room on the sand rather than the road: here the difference is the whole point of coming.
facts: From the Kendwa Rocks cluster north to the Kilindi headland
About 20 minutes on foot, end to end
A madafu, opened for you by a beach vendor
Constant vendor traffic: it is public beach throughout

q-kendwa-road.name: Kendwa Road
q-kendwa-road.teaser: One block inland: the dukas, the cheaper beds, and a sandy turning down to every hotel gate
q-kendwa-road.story: Behind the sand runs the service road, parallel to the beach and one block inland, with a turning down to every hotel gate. This is the half of Kendwa that the brochures crop out and the half you will use most: the small shops, the dukas, the kitchens without sea frontage, and the rooms that cost less because they are a two-minute walk from the water instead of on it. After dark it changes character. There are no street lights and the surface is soft sand, so a five-minute stroll becomes a slow walk by torchlight, which is part of its pleasure if you are ready for it.
q-kendwa-road.why: Stay here, eat here, and spend the money you saved on the sand side.
facts: Parallel to the beach, one block inland
Dukas, small shops and the cheaper beds
A torch after dark: the road is unlit
Sandy underfoot, so expect to walk it slowly

q-kilindi-end.name: The Kilindi end
q-kilindi-end.teaser: Twenty minutes north of the bars the beach empties, and fifteen white domes stand in fifty acres
q-kilindi-end.story: Walk north from the bars and within twenty minutes the beach has emptied out entirely. The sand thins, the hotels stop advertising themselves, and the gardens of Kilindi run down to the water, its white domed pavilions showing through the green. They were built as a private house for Benny Andersson of ABBA before Elewana took the property on, and the venue card tells that story. What matters here is the stillness: this is the quietest stretch of sand on the cape, the place to come when Kendwa Rocks is loud, and the end of the evening walk described under walks.
q-kilindi-end.why: Come for the empty sand: it is the one stretch of Kendwa where you may have the beach to yourself.
facts: North end of Kendwa beach, toward the headland
About 20 minutes on foot north from the bars
The domes seen from the water's edge

q-nungwi-strip.name: Nungwi west — the strip
q-nungwi-strip.teaser: A few hundred metres of driftwood bars and dive desks, where the boats leave for Mnemba and the bank
q-nungwi-strip.story: Nungwi's western edge is the busiest sand on the north tip: driftwood bars, boutique hotels, three dive centres and, every evening, the sunset crowd, all packed along a few hundred metres of west-facing beach south of the village centre. Cholo's and Langi Langi are two of its names. In the morning the strip has a second job: the dive boats for Mnemba and Leven Bank load here, so this is where you book, kit up and wade out. Two hundred metres inland a village of several thousand people goes about its day, and the two are a whole world apart.
q-nungwi-strip.why: Base yourself here if you dive: the boats leave from the beach in front of you.
facts: West-facing beach, south of the village centre
Sunset for the bars; early morning for the boats
The dive desks that run Mnemba and Leven Bank

q-nungwi-village.name: Nungwi village
q-nungwi-village.teaser: Two hundred metres inland: mosques, dukas, fruit sellers and kitchens with seven tables
q-nungwi-village.story: This is where several thousand people actually live, and where the good cheap food is. Turn your back on the bar strip and walk two hundred metres inland to the main road: mosques, dukas, fruit sellers, and kitchens of seven tables where lunch costs a fraction of what it does on the sand, Machnoo among them. The village asks one thing of you, which is to dress for it. On Friday around midday the village closes for prayers, and the lanes go quiet.
q-nungwi-village.why: Eat lunch here at least once: the village is the place the beach exists to serve.
facts: Inland of the beach, around the main road
Shoulders and knees covered, for men as well as women
Friday around midday, when the village is at prayers
The small kitchens, Machnoo among them

q-working-beach.name: The working beach
q-working-beach.teaser: Past the last bar the beach changes job: hulls on the sand, an auction at dawn, grills after six
q-working-beach.story: Keep walking north past the last bar and the beach stops being for visitors. Dhow hulls stand on the open sand. At first light the fish market runs its auction on the landing; after six in the evening the same stretch smells of charcoal from the grills. It is perhaps four hundred metres long and it is the most interesting ground on the cape, precisely because it is not an attraction. People are working. Ask before you photograph anybody. The way to see it properly is the first-light walk under walks.
q-working-beach.why: Go once at dawn and once after six: same sand, two different trades.
facts: North of the Nungwi hotel strip, toward the point
First light for the auction; after 18:00 for the grills
See the first-light walk under walks

t-water-stays.name: Why the water stays
t-water-stays.teaser: On the east coast the sea walks a kilometre out twice a day; at Kendwa it moves a few metres
t-water-stays.story: On Unguja's east coast, at Paje, Jambiani and Michamvi, the fringing reef sits one to one and a half kilometres offshore over almost flat ground. When the tide drops, the sea retreats all the way to the reef crest and the flats dry into a shallow, walkable moonscape. Beautiful, and you cannot swim, twice a day, every day. Kendwa's seabed falls away steeply within a few metres of the sand. The same tidal range on a steep profile moves the waterline a short distance instead of a kilometre, so there is water deep enough to swim at any state of the tide.
t-water-stays.why: This is the honest reason to choose this coast over the prettier east: you can swim when you want to, not when the moon allows.
facts: Seabed drops away within a few metres of the sand
Reef 1 to 1.5 km out; the flats between dry at low water

t-sunset-face.name: And why it faces the sunset
t-sunset-face.teaser: The second accident of geometry: open water to the west, past Daloni and the long shape of Tumbatu
t-sunset-face.story: Kendwa sits on the north-west shoulder of the island, about three kilometres short of the northern point. That aspect gives it open water to the west, past the small island of Daloni and the long low shape of Tumbatu, and therefore the sunset. The great east-coast beaches face the other way, toward the sunrise across a reef. Put the steep shelf together with the western aspect and you have the whole explanation for Unguja's north-west hotel economy: water to swim in all day, and the sun going down into it at the end.
t-sunset-face.why: Look west at dusk and you are reading the map: Daloni first, Tumbatu behind it, nothing but sea beyond.

t-spring-tides.name: Spring tides — new and full moon
t-spring-tides.teaser: Twice a month the sea here pulls back far enough to walk the reef, and fish gets cheaper
t-spring-tides.story: Around new and full moon the tidal range is at its widest: lows lower, highs higher. For a few days the reef flats north and east of the point expose far enough to walk. That is when the octopus gatherers go out on foot (their story is in sea stories). More boats land more fish, so the price at the Nungwi market drops. Walk the flats in hard soles and watch where you put your hands: stonefish are real, and the coral rag is sharp. If you have a choice of weeks, take the one straddling a full or new moon.
t-spring-tides.why: Book the week around a full or new moon: widest reef walk, biggest landings, cheapest fish.
facts: The reef flats north and east of the point
Stonefish, and the sharp coral rag
Check a Zanzibar tide table before you book the week, not after

t-fifty-minutes.name: The landing walks around the day
t-fifty-minutes.teaser: The boats come back on the tide, not the clock, and the tide is fifty minutes later every day
t-fifty-minutes.story: Tides run to a lunar day of roughly twenty-four hours and fifty minutes, so each high and each low arrives about fifty minutes later than the day before. The fishermen work to that, not to a timetable. This is why 'the market is at six' is wrong advice, however confidently it is given: the market is at whatever hour the tide gives it, and the hour walks forward through the week. Monday's dawn landing can be a mid-morning landing by the weekend. The fix is one question, asked on your first morning to anyone pulling a boat up the sand.
t-fifty-minutes.why: Ask a fisherman on day one when they go out tomorrow, then add fifty minutes for each day after.
facts: Each tide comes about 50 minutes later than the day before
When are you going out tomorrow, on your first morning
Add 50 minutes for each following day

w-kendwa-nungwi.name: Kendwa to Nungwi on the sand
w-kendwa-nungwi.teaser: Three kilometres of firm sand and a rocky shoulder that the tide opens and shuts twice a day
w-kendwa-nungwi.story: The best short walk on the cape, and the one to plan properly. At low water the sand is firm the whole way, the path hugs the water, and the rocky headland between the two beaches, about three hundred metres of it, is passable. At high water it is not, and people do get caught by the returning tide on this stretch. Read the table for the return as well. Never do it after dark, in either direction. If the door has shut, the back road is longer, unlit and sandy; take a taxi or a boda instead.
w-kendwa-nungwi.why: Time it to the tide and you arrive in Nungwi on foot along the water's edge, the best half hour on the cape.
facts: Firm sand, then the rocky shoulder of the headland
On a falling tide, from about two hours before low; never after dark
The headland crossing between the two beaches
A tide table for the way back as well as the way out
If the tide has shut it
Taxi or boda on the inland road, about 10 minutes; agree the fare first

w-last-hour.name: The last hour on Kendwa sand
w-last-hour.teaser: North toward the domes as the light goes: no viewing deck, no ticket, people just stop in the sea
w-last-hour.story: Start at the Kendwa Rocks cluster and walk north toward the Kilindi headland. Within five minutes the crowd thins, then the hotels stop and the beach is only beach. Because this coast faces north-west and the shelf is steep, the sun goes down into open water past Tumbatu and you can be standing in the sea while it happens. Nobody announces it and there is nowhere to buy a ticket; people simply stop and look. It is short, too, because the tropics do not do long dusks. Turn round when the light goes orange and you are back among the bars in time for a drink.
w-last-hour.why: Be in the water, not on a sunbed, when the sun touches the sea.
facts: Sunset falls roughly 18:15 to 18:45 all year at this latitude
The sun going down past Tumbatu, seen standing in the sea

w-first-light.name: First light: landing, yards and the point
w-first-light.teaser: Boats landing in the half dark, a shouted auction, hulls on the sand, then the lighthouse
w-first-light.story: Walk north up Nungwi beach in the half dark to where the market works. The boats land on the tide, so the hour moves forward about fifty minutes a day; ask the evening before. Then stand still. The auction is shouted, fast and over quickly, and it is the best twenty minutes of the week. Keep going: the dhow yards share the same working stretch of sand, the hulls standing in frame, and if you carry on you reach the point and the lighthouse. Go before nine, before the heat stops the work. It is a workplace, not a show; the yard etiquette is in craft.
w-first-light.why: Stand still at the auction for twenty minutes and say nothing: that is the whole skill.
facts: Nungwi beach, north of the last bar
First light, timed by the tide; done before 09:00
The auction, shouted and over quickly
Shillings in small notes if you mean to buy

w-village-lighthouse.name: Nungwi village to the lighthouse
w-village-lighthouse.teaser: Through the mosques and dukas to the island's northern tip, a world away from the bars
w-village-lighthouse.story: Leave the beach and go inland, through the village proper: the dukas, the fruit sellers, the mosques, the kitchens of seven tables, then out along the lanes to the 1926 tower on the island's northern point, with the turtle pond beside it. It is two hundred metres from the bar strip and a completely different island. Greet people as you pass. Buy something small from a duka on the way, a cold drink or a bag of fruit, which is the easiest way to be a guest rather than a spectator.
w-village-lighthouse.why: Walk it slowly and buy something on the way: the village notices who stops.
facts: Nungwi village, inland from the bar strip
Village lanes, then the coral of the point
Any time except Friday around midday, when the village is at prayers
The lighthouse and the turtle pond at the end

r-leven.name: Leven Bank
r-leven.teaser: Two nautical miles of reef in open channel, walls past 160 metres, and only on the right tide
r-leven.story: Out in the Pemba Channel north of the island lies a submerged bank around two nautical miles long, topped with coral and sand patches, its walls dropping past a hundred and sixty metres. Big water, big fish, and the current that brings them is the reason it can only be dived on certain tides: the attraction and the hazard in the same breath. Every centre here says the same thing: experienced divers only, and not as your first dive of a trip. The name very likely honours HMS Leven, which charted this coast in the 1820s, though we could not confirm it from a primary source.
r-leven.why: A centre that promises Leven tomorrow regardless of the tide is a centre to walk away from; take the cancellation as professionalism.
facts: Pemba Channel, north of the island
Experienced divers only, never your first dive of a trip
On a tide, not a date, with a centre in Kendwa or Nungwi
The dive desk to show you why, on the tide table

r-mnemba.name: Mnemba Atoll
r-mnemba.teaser: A private island you cannot land on, ringed by the best snorkelling reachable from the north tip
r-mnemba.story: Off the north-east coast, Mnemba is a marine conservation area around an island that is a private lodge. You cannot land: any boatman promising a beach stop there is selling something he cannot deliver. What you get instead is the easiest good diving and the best snorkelling reachable from here, and turtles seen wild, unfed and unpenned. &Beyond, which operates the island, runs a marine programme there, with coral-reef restoration in progress. Book through a dive centre rather than a beach tout and take an early departure, before the wind gets up.
r-mnemba.why: Go for the turtles in open water: this is the honest alternative to any pond.
facts: About 1 h 15 by road to the Matemwe launch, or by boat from Nungwi
US$10 a person conservation fee, on top of the trip (seen Aug 2026)
An early departure, before the wind
Through a dive centre, not a beach tout
Pay for a landing on the island: it is private

r-tumbatu-reefs.name: Tumbatu and the shallow reefs
r-tumbatu-reefs.teaser: Where the boat goes when Leven Bank is off, and not a consolation prize
r-tumbatu-reefs.story: The reefs off Tumbatu, and sites such as Wattabomi and Magic Reef, are the shallower northern dives: gentler water, plenty of coral, and suitable for every level. When Leven Bank is off, which it frequently is, this is where the day goes, and a good divemaster will make you glad of it. One distinction matters: diving the water off Tumbatu is not the same as setting foot on the island, which needs the elders' permission (see Tumbatu under landmarks).
r-tumbatu-reefs.why: Do not sulk when the bank is cancelled: the shallow reefs are where you actually look at the coral.
facts: Wattabomi, Magic Reef and the reefs off Tumbatu
Daily from both Kendwa and Nungwi
Confuse diving off Tumbatu with landing on it

r-humpbacks.name: The humpbacks
r-humpbacks.teaser: Humpbacks come up from South African water with calves alongside and pass through this channel
r-humpbacks.story: Every year humpback whales move north from the cold water off South Africa toward the warmer tropics, calves alongside, arriving here from late July and turning back south through September and October. They are seen in the bay off Nungwi and in the Zanzibar Channel, with the most sightings in August and September. The north coast stays calm in this season, which is exactly why the boats can go out and look. The difference between a good trip and a bad one is the skipper: one keeps a legal distance and cuts the engine; the other chases.
r-humpbacks.why: Choose the boat by its skipper: the one who keeps his distance and cuts the engine.
facts: From late July; heading south through September and October
The bay off Nungwi and the Zanzibar Channel
With a dive centre, not a beach tout
Whether the skipper keeps a legal distance and cuts the engine

r-two-seasons.name: Kusi and kaskazi
r-two-seasons.teaser: In the kusi months the sky goes hard blue, the seaweed leaves and the visibility peaks
r-two-seasons.story: The kusi, the southerly trade, blows from about June to October. It keeps the humidity down and the sky hard blue, and it pushes nutrient-rich water across the northern banks, which is what brings the big pelagics in. Visibility reaches its annual best. The water sits around the mid-twenties Celsius, cool enough that a three-millimetre suit earns its place on a second or third dive, and the drifting seaweed that fouls the beaches in other months is largely gone. The same wind roughens the east coast, so the north-west is the side to be on. December to February, under the kaskazi, is the other dry window.
r-two-seasons.why: For diving, aim for the kusi months: clearest water of the year, on the sheltered side.
facts: About June to October: dry, clear, best visibility
Around the mid-twenties Celsius in the kusi
A 3 mm suit for repeat dives

r-turtles.name: The turtles, honestly
r-turtles.teaser: Two ponds on this cape take money for turtles; the reef at Mnemba takes none
r-turtles.story: Green and hawksbill turtles are common on the northern reefs and routinely seen on a Mnemba dive or snorkel. On land, two paying turtle attractions stand within a few hundred metres of each other, and they are not equivalent. Mnarani, by the lighthouse, has the longer record (its card is under landmarks). Baraka Natural Aquarium is the one you will be offered most. Its own site describes rescue, rehabilitation and release. Visitor accounts dispute that in strong terms: animals handled and ridden, a small crowded pond, turtles bought from fishermen, no evidence of releases produced on request. We could not settle it, and we will not pretend to.
r-turtles.why: If you want turtles and want to be sure, get in the water at Mnemba.
facts: On a Mnemba dive or snorkel
US$10 each to swim with, feed or see the zoo; daily 08:00 to 18:00 (seen Aug 2026)
Baraka's site claims releases; visitor accounts allege handling, crowding and no releases
Mnarani for the conservation story, Mnemba for the animals

l-lighthouse.name: Ras Nungwi Lighthouse
l-lighthouse.teaser: Stand at the island's northern tip at dusk and watch a thirteen-mile light come on
l-lighthouse.story: A white three-stage square stone tower with a red lantern, on the island's northern point: fourteen metres high, focal plane eighteen metres, range thirteen nautical miles, built in 1926. There is no public access, and you do not need it. Go at dusk, stand with your back to the tower, and you can see both halves of this coast at once: the bar strip and the sunset on one side, the quiet bay and the working sea on the other. Then the light comes on above you. The best five minutes on the cape.
l-lighthouse.why: Be there as the light comes on: both coasts and the first beam, in five minutes.
facts: Ras Nungwi, the island's northern point, beside the turtle pond
Exterior only: no public access to the tower
Five minutes, or as long as the dusk lasts
Both coasts from one spot, with your back to the tower

l-mnarani.name: Mnarani turtle pond
l-mnarani.teaser: A tidal pool in the coral rag, with rehabilitated turtles released into the surf every February
l-mnarani.story: In 1993 Nungwi villagers and conservationists set up a refuge for green and hawksbill turtles caught in fishing nets. The pond is a natural tidal pool, separated from the sea by a few metres of old reef and flushed by every tide, with separate pools for hatchlings, juveniles and injured animals, a pier and an information pavilion. Each February the rehabilitated turtles are released in public. Since June 2016 it has also run a recycling project, Trash to Treasures. Be clear about what it is: still a captive pond with paying visitors, and the animals are handled. The name means 'at the lighthouse', and it is.
l-mnarani.why: Time a February visit for the release, the one moment the pond makes its case.
facts: Beside the lighthouse at Ras Nungwi
The separate pools for hatchlings, juveniles and injured animals
A captive pond where the animals are handled; if that is your line, see them wild at Mnemba
l-mnarani.maps_query: Mnarani Marine Turtles Conservation Pond Nungwi

l-coral-rag.name: The coral rag
l-coral-rag.teaser: The grey, razor-edged rock under your feet is a dead reef, lifted out of the sea, and it cuts
l-coral-rag.story: The grey, pitted, razor-edged rock at the point and behind both beaches is fossil coral: the reef this island once was, lifted out of the sea and dead. Once you see it you see it everywhere. It is why the turtle pond exists as a natural pool, why there is barely any soil, and why the vegetation behind the sand is scrub rather than forest. Walk it in something with a hard sole. A slip on coral rag opens a wound that heals slowly in this climate.
l-coral-rag.why: Look closely at the rock by the lighthouse: you are standing on a reef.
facts: All around the point and behind both beaches
Walk it barefoot or in flip-flops

l-tumbatu.name: Tumbatu
l-tumbatu.teaser: A medieval Swahili state four kilometres offshore, and a community that keeps its door shut
l-tumbatu.story: The long low island west of Kendwa at sunset is the third largest in the archipelago, about eight kilometres by two or three, with its own dialect of Swahili. Between roughly 1100 and 1300 Jongowe was among the largest settlements on the whole Zanzibar coast, and ruins from that time stand at Makutani. It is the most historically important thing you can see from Kendwa sand and the one you are least entitled to walk into. Anyone not from Tumbatu, Zanzibaris included, needs written permission from the village elders, and visits go with an approved guide who seeks that blessing first. Do not hire a boat and turn up.
l-tumbatu.why: Go properly or not at all: the reserve is deliberate, and it is theirs to keep.
facts: By boat from Mkokotoni, with a permit and an approved guide arranged days ahead
Written, from the village elders, for anyone not from Tumbatu
The ruins at Makutani, on a permitted visit
Any west-facing point on Kendwa sand

c-christ-church.name: Christ Church & the slave-market memorial
c-christ-church.teaser: A cathedral raised on the island's last open slave market, the holding chambers still beneath
c-christ-church.story: Stone Town's Anglican cathedral was built on the site of the last open slave market on the island, and the altar is said to stand where the whipping post stood. Beside it, beneath the adjacent buildings, the underground holding chambers survive: low, dark and deliberately hard to be in. Stoop inside for a minute and the spice-island story changes shape. This is the honest half of a day in Stone Town, and it is not optional if you intend to enjoy the cloves. Lukmaan, where you will eat lunch afterwards, is a few minutes' walk away.
c-christ-church.why: Go down into the chambers, even briefly: the low ceiling teaches what no plaque can.
c-christ-church.maps_query: Christ Church Cathedral Stone Town Zanzibar

c-old-fort.name: The Old Fort
c-old-fort.teaser: An Omani fort on a Portuguese footprint, standing at the gate of the night market
c-old-fort.story: The fort on the Stone Town seafront was built by the Omanis over the site of an earlier Portuguese chapel, so its walls hold two empires in one footprint. Today the inside is a courtyard of craft stalls and an amphitheatre that hosts events some evenings. The stalls sell curios; the building is the point. Step out of the gate and Forodhani is immediately beside it, which makes the fort the natural start of any evening on the waterfront.
c-old-fort.why: Give it twenty minutes before Forodhani: it orients the whole seafront.
facts: Late afternoon, before the night market
The building itself, more than the stalls

c-house-of-wonders.name: House of Wonders
c-house-of-wonders.teaser: The sultan's palace that held the last sewn ship, until the roof came down in December 2020
c-house-of-wonders.story: The sultan's seafront palace was once the tallest building in East Africa and the first on the island with electricity and a lift. Part of it collapsed in December 2020, and it has stood under restoration ever since; when we checked in October 2026 no reopening date had been announced. You cannot go in, and anyone offering a tour inside is not selling what they say. It matters here for one reason. It housed the Dhow Cultures exhibition and with it Shungwaya, the 2003 reconstruction of a sewn mtepe. When the roof came down the ship was moved outdoors, and it has been weathering ever since.
c-house-of-wonders.why: Walk past on the Forodhani promenade: the shut building is the present state of this island's maritime memory.
facts: Stone Town seafront, on the Forodhani walk
Closed to the public since the 2020 collapse; exterior only, no reopening date announced (seen Oct 2026)
Nothing to pay: there is no entry
A few minutes from the promenade
Pay anyone for a tour inside
